figures.title: One Schmidt-spectrum path, several entanglement lenses
figures.reader_question: What unifies the many entanglement metrics?
figures.answer: The ordered Schmidt-spectrum path is the common latent object; metric projections form a trajectory atlas with both shared coarse morphology and informative local competition.
figures.caption: One ordered Schmidt-spectrum path generates several nonlinear entanglement trajectories. Their atlas can retain shared coarse morphology while allowing local metric competition. Majorization identifies the sector in which Schur-concave metrics must agree; incomparable spectra leave room for valid contradictions.
figures.alt_text: Flow diagram. A Schmidt-spectrum path feeds four lenses labelled H one-half, H one, H two class, and H infinity. The lenses join in a trajectory atlas, which branches to shared coarse morphology and local metric competition. Text states that majorization forces agreement on comparable spectra and incomparability allows contradictions.

figures.title: Exact metric arenas
figures.reader_question: What part of the comparison is exact?
figures.answer: Majorization extremizers give exact fixed-largest-eigenvalue feasible envelopes and a common boundary-relative stage.
figures.caption: Exact finite-dimensional feasible arenas at n=20 and reduced dimension d=1024. The horizontal coordinate is normalized min-entropy, equivalent to the largest Schmidt value. Concentrated and equal-tail spectra give the exact lower and upper boundaries for von Neumann entropy, the order-two class, and pure-state logarithmic negativity. Orange points are the included n=20 observations.
figures.alt_text: Three panels plot normalized von Neumann entropy, linear entropy, and pure-state log-negativity against normalized min-entropy. Each panel contains a blue feasible region bounded by a stepped lower curve and smooth upper curve, with orange data points inside.

figures.title: Metric robustness is hierarchical
figures.reader_question: How strong is the cross-metric invariance, and what does not survive?
figures.answer: A dominant normalized common mode and stable coarse rankings coexist with weak exact-turn agreement.
figures.caption: Metric robustness is strong but hierarchical. The first normalized common mode explains 90.3 percent of variance, with a model-stratified design-cluster sensitivity interval. Pairwise rank agreement persists across sizes. Full-path arc-length and vertical-variation rankings are stable, whereas exact turn-count agreement is weak.
figures.alt_text: Three-panel quantitative summary. Panel A shows a common mode near ninety percent, a contrast mode near nine percent, and a small residual. Panel B shows three cross-metric correlation curves from n equals ten to twenty. Panel C shows high full-path arc-length rank agreement, metric-pair-dependent vertical-variation agreement, and low exact turn-count agreement.

figures.title: Majorization and metric competition
figures.reader_question: How can valid metrics contradict one another?
figures.answer: Incomparable spectra can reverse metric order; all selected empirical competition events occur in the incomparable sector.
figures.caption: The trajectory atlas explains consensus and contradiction. An explicit incomparable spectrum pair reverses the ordering of different Renyi sectors. In the selected full-spectrum audit, competition occurs only among incomparable transitions. The overall competition rate varies strongly across the four model families.
figures.alt_text: Three panels. Panel A compares two four-entry spectra and lists which one has larger H one, H two, H one-half, and H infinity. Panel B is a stacked bar chart showing no metric competition in majorization-compatible increases or decreases and some competition for incomparable transitions. Panel C shows competition rates increasing from QCA to random-field XXZ.

figures.title: Model morphology and fingerprint limits
figures.reader_question: Do trajectories carry model information, and how far does it generalize?
figures.answer: Model-centroid morphology is distinct and generalizes across held-out sizes; individual unseen conditions remain much harder.
figures.caption: Model-level morphology is stronger than individual fingerprinting. The n=20 model-centroid trajectories occupy distinct regions of largest-Schmidt-value versus common-mode space. The classification panel separates the contribution of the shared horizontal coordinate from vertical metric information and shows the sharp drop under unseen individual conditions.
figures.alt_text: Two panels. The left panel plots four model-centroid paths. The right panel separates full-path, vertical-only, and lambda-max-only held-out classification: model-centroid full-path accuracy is about 0.875 same metric and 0.674 cross metric, while individual double-holdout performance is near 0.33 to 0.36 and does not beat the lambda-max baseline.
